analysis.title: USD: Watchful of tech and the midterms
key_insights: Nomura has begun stepping back from its long USD view since 16 October, mainly because of US tech weakness and slower US portfolio inflows. The shift shows up in a new short USD/JPY recommendation and higher conviction on short USD/CNH.

The prior tactical shift (from 11 September) moved away from the softer USD camp held since 17 July. It rested on higher US inflation, Fed tightening uncertainty (risk of more hikes), rising energy prices and higher global yields.
Tech concerns have two parts. One is credit risk among small, leveraged tech companies. The other is whether Mag-7 capex expansion continues and is supported by strong revenues.

Bloomberg data (26 October) show 15.2% of US tech company loans at distressed levels (10% over SOFR) on a USD278.3bn sample, approaching highs of the year. US HY credit default swap spreads have risen steadily over the past month and are also approaching highs of the year.
Foreign holdings of US portfolio assets stand at USD40.9trn as of Q2 2026. Tech weakness could cut foreign equity inflows and raise fears over this heavy foreign positioning.

Mag-7 earnings are the near-term focus: Microsoft and Alphabet (28 October), Amazon (29 October), Apple (2 November), Nvidia (17 November). Nomura sees asymmetry toward a more negative market reaction if earnings disappoint, given investor nervousness.

A negative earnings reaction would likely add medium-term support to a weaker USD. Major global central banks, pension funds, sovereign funds and asset managers plan to reduce USD assets, made worse by Trump's de-globalisation and nationalist policies and geopolitical aggression.

Nomura's economics team base case is a 90% probability of Democrats taking the House (Polymarket 92%, 27 October) and around 60% for a Democratic sweep of both chambers. Polymarket has Democrats controlling the Senate at 67%.

A Democratic sweep is the more negative scenario for USD and US equities, at least initially. Most Democratic candidates in GOP-held Toss Up states (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Texas) have pushed for more data center regulation. Other risks are less large-scale fiscal stimulus and more congressional investigations of the Trump administration.

If Democrats win the House while the Senate stays Republican, USD and US equities could get initial temporary support because a sweep is already priced by polls and Polymarket. After that, risks remain from tech/AI regulation, fiscal negotiations, more continuing resolutions, shutdown risk and debt ceiling concerns.

A Republican-held Senate could raise Fed independence concerns because the administration could confirm Fed nominees. Barkin (Richmond), Williams (NY Fed) and Daly (SF) are set to retire in January 2028, June 2028 and October 2028.
